a: and there was Raguel, sitting at the door of his courtyard.
t: Raguel at the door, or Sarah?
p: In Sinaiticus the travelers find Raguel at his door. In Vaticanus, followed by the KJV, Sarah comes out to meet them.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ εὗρον αὐτὸν καθήμενον παρὰ τὴν θύραν τῆς αὐλῆς
readings.en: and they found him sitting by the door of the courtyard
readings.plain: and there was Raguel, sitting at the door of his courtyard.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: καὶ Σάρρα δὲ ὑπήντησεν αὐτῷ
readings.en: and Sarah met him
readings.plain: and Sarah came out to meet him.

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. In Vaticanus Sarah greets the guests first, echoing the well scenes of Genesis 24 and 29.

a: my brother Tobit
p: Sinaiticus writes the name in the form it usually uses for Tobias. Vaticanus has "my cousin Tobit."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Τωβεία, τῷ ἀδελφῷ μου
readings.en: Tobia(s), my brother
readings.plain: my brother Tobit

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: Τωβεὶτ τῷ ἀνεψιῷ μου
readings.en: Tobit, my cousin
readings.plain: my cousin Tobit

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus but reads the name as Tobit. Raguel is comparing the young man with his kinsman, who must be the father, and in 7:7 Sinaiticus uses the same spelling for Tobias, so the scribe's spelling of the two names is not reliable here. Vaticanus confirms that Tobit is meant.

a: Edna asked them
p: In Sinaiticus Edna leads the questioning; in Vaticanus Raguel does.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἠρώτησεν αὐτοὺς Ἔδνα
readings.en: Edna asked them
readings.plain: Edna asked them

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: ἠρώτησεν αὐτοὺς Ῥαγουήλ
readings.en: Raguel asked them
readings.plain: Raguel asked them

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus, the base text. Its version gives Edna a fuller part, and in 7:4–5 the travelers answer "her" (αὐτῇ), which fits Edna as the questioner. Vaticanus, followed by the KJV, makes Raguel the speaker throughout.

a: Together they said
p: In Sinaiticus both say Amen. In Vaticanus Sarah says it with Tobias, and in the Vulgate she prays aloud.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ εἶπαν μεθ᾽ ἑαυτῶν
readings.en: and they said together
readings.plain: Together they said

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: καὶ εἶπεν μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and she said with him
readings.plain: She said with him

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Jerome, about AD 400), verse 8:10, and Douay-Rheims
readings.orig: Dixit quoque Sara: Miserere nobis Domine, miserere nobis, et consenescamus ambo pariter sani
readings.en: Sara also said: Have mercy on us, O Lord, have mercy on us, and let us grow old both together in health (Douay)
readings.plain: Sarah also said, "Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us, and let us both grow old together in health." Together they said

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. The two Greek forms agree that Sarah joins in the Amen; the Vulgate gives her a prayer of her own, which many Catholic wedding books printed.

a: Let them bless you forever.
p: Sinaiticus is brief. Vaticanus names the saints, all creatures, the angels and the chosen.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: εὐλογείτωσάν σε εἰς πάντας τοὺς αἰῶνας
readings.en: let them bless you for all ages
readings.plain: Let them bless you forever.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: εὐλογείτωσάν σε οἱ ἅγιοί σου καὶ πᾶσαι αἱ κτίσεις σου, πάντες οἱ ἄγγελοί σου καὶ οἱ ἐκλεκτοί σου εὐλογείτωσάν σε εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας
readings.en: let your saints and all your creatures, all your angels and your chosen ones bless you forever
readings.plain: Let your holy ones and all your creatures bless you; let all your angels and your chosen ones bless you forever.

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. Its "them" has no stated subject, and Vaticanus may have filled it in. Swete's apparatus notes that a corrector of Vaticanus and Codex Alexandrinus add "pure and holy" (καθαρα και αγια) after "every blessing"; Sinaiticus already has "pure" (καθαρᾷ).

a: Woe is me
t: "Woe is me" or "I care for nothing"?
p: Sinaiticus has Anna cry "Woe is me." Vaticanus, followed by the KJV, has "Does nothing matter to me?"

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Οὐαί μοι
readings.en: Woe to me
readings.plain: Woe is me

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: Οὐ μέλει μοι
readings.en: It is no concern to me / Do I not care?
readings.plain: Nothing matters to me now

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. The two Greek words look much alike (ΟΥΑΙΜΟΙ and ΟΥΜΕΛΕΙΜΟΙ), so one is probably a copyist's change of the other. "Woe is me" fits a mother's lament; the KJV reads "Now I care for nothing, my son."

a: Day after day she ran out and kept scanning the road her son had gone by, and she listened to no one. At sunset she came indoors, and all night long she wailed and cried and got no sleep.
p: Sinaiticus says Anna watched the road and could not sleep. Vaticanus says she ate no bread by day.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἐκπηδήσασα περιεβλέπετο τὴν ὁδὸν ᾗ ᾤχετο ὁ υἱὸς αὐτῆς καθ᾽ ἡμέραν καὶ οὐκ ἐπείθετο οὐδενί
readings.en: rushing out, she looked around at the road her son had gone, every day, and believed no one
readings.plain: Day after day she ran out and kept scanning the road her son had gone by, and she listened to no one. At sunset she came indoors, and all night long she wailed and cried and got no sleep.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: ἡμέρας τε ἄρτον οὐκ ἤσθιεν, τὰς δὲ νύκτας οὐ διελίμπανεν θρηνοῦσα Τωβείαν τὸν υἱὸν αὐτῆς
readings.en: by day she ate no bread, and through the nights she did not stop mourning her son Tobias
readings.plain: Every day she went out to the road by which he had gone away. By day she ate no bread, and through the nights she never stopped mourning for her son Tobias.

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus, the base text. Vaticanus, followed by the KJV, adds a fast; both describe the same grief.

a: Go to your father-in-law's house.
p: Sinaiticus sends Sarah to her father-in-law. Vaticanus tells her to honor her parents-in-law.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Ὕπαγε πρὸς τὸν πενθερόν σου
readings.en: Go to your father-in-law
readings.plain: Go to your father-in-law's house.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: Τίμα τοὺς πενθερούς σου
readings.en: Honor your parents-in-law
readings.plain: Honor your father-in-law and mother-in-law.

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. The Vaticanus form, which the KJV follows ("Honour thy father and thy mother in law"), applies the commandment to honor parents (Exodus 20:12) to a bride's new family, a reading often used in Christian marriage sermons.

a: And the dog came along, following them.
p: Sinaiticus says "the Lord" went along behind them, almost surely a slip for "the dog."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: καὶ συνῆλθεν ὁ κύων ὄπισθεν αὐτῶν
readings.en: and the dog came along behind them
readings.plain: And the dog came along, following them.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ συνῆλθεν αὐτοῖς ὁ κύριος ἐκ τῶν ὀπίσω αὐτοῦ καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτῆς
readings.en: and the Lord came along with them, behind him and her son
readings.plain: And the Lord came along with them, behind him and her son.

why: Here the Plain follows Vaticanus. The dog set out with Tobias in Sinaiticus itself (6:2), and ὁ κύων (the dog) and ὁ κύριος (the Lord, often written ΚΣ in manuscripts) are easily confused; the rest of the Sinaiticus line ("behind him and her son") is also garbled. Most editors make the same correction.

a: His eyes smarted, and he rubbed them.
p: Swete's Sinaiticus has no 11:12. The Plain supplies it from Vaticanus. This may be only a difference in where the verses are divided.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: ὡς δὲ συνεδήχθησαν, διέτριψε τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: when they stung, he rubbed his eyes
readings.plain: His eyes smarted, and he rubbed them.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete (no verse 11:12)
readings.en: (nothing; 11:11 ends with καὶ ἐπέδωκεν, 'and it took effect')

why: Sinaiticus is not missing a block of text here as it is in 13:6–10. Its 11:11 ends with καὶ ἐπέδωκεν, "and it took effect," and its 11:13 goes straight on to the peeling of the white films, so the stinging and rubbing of Vaticanus 11:12 have no exact match. The Plain gives Vaticanus's short line so that every verse is present, as the site's numbering requires; read together, 11:11–13 lose nothing either way.

a: he flaked the white films off
p: Sinaiticus says only that he peeled with both hands, with no object. Vaticanus names the white films.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: ἐλεπίσθη ἀπὸ τῶν κανθῶν τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτοῦ τὰ λευκώματα
readings.en: the white films were peeled from the corners of his eyes
readings.plain: he flaked the white films off

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ ἀπελέπισεν ἑκατέραις ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and he peeled with both his hands
readings.plain: he peeled them off

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus but supplies the object "the white films" from Vaticanus and from Raphael's words in 11:8, since English needs one. The sense is the same.

a: He struck me
t: "He struck me" or "you struck me and had mercy"?
p: Sinaiticus speaks of God: "he struck me." Vaticanus, followed by the KJV, speaks to God and adds mercy.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ὅτι αὐτὸς ἐμαστίγωσέν με
readings.en: for he himself struck me
readings.plain: He struck me

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: ὅτι ἐμαστίγωσας καὶ ἠλέησάς με
readings.en: for you struck me and had mercy on me
readings.plain: You struck me, and you had mercy on me

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. Vaticanus states outright the pairing of striking and mercy that both texts make in the hymn (13:2, 13:5).

a: Nadab
p: Sinaiticus spells the nephew's name Nabad here, but Nadab in 14:10. Vaticanus calls him Nasbas.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus at 14:10, the same man's name, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Ναδάβ
readings.en: Nadab
readings.plain: Nadab

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete, at 11:18
readings.orig: Ναβὰδ
readings.en: Nabad
readings.plain: Nabad

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: Νασβᾶς
readings.en: Nasbas
readings.plain: Nasbas

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, corrector (ℵc.a), Swete's note on 11:18
readings.orig: Αχεικαρ ℵ*] Αχεια- | χαρος ℵc.a | οι εξαδελφοι ℵ*] ο -φος ℵc.a (Swete's note: the corrector writes Ahiqar as Achiacharus and makes "nephews" singular)
readings.en: Achiacharus … his nephew (Nadab unchanged)
readings.plain: Nadab

why: The Plain corrects Sinaiticus here to its own spelling in 14:10, so the reader meets one name for one man. Nabad looks like two letters swapped. The Aramaic Story of Ahiqar calls the nephew Nadin, which is closer to Nadab.

a: Tobias's wedding was celebrated with gladness for seven days.
p: Sinaiticus has no 11:19. Vaticanus and the Vulgate have a seven-day feast in Nineveh.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: καὶ ἤχθη ὁ γάμος Τωβεία μετ᾽ εὐφροσύνης ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας
readings.en: and Tobias's wedding was kept with gladness seven days
readings.plain: Tobias's wedding was celebrated with gladness for seven days.

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Jerome), verse 11:21
readings.orig: Et per septem dies epulantes, omnes cum gaudio magno gavisi sunt
readings.en: and for seven days they feasted and rejoiced all with great joy (Douay)
readings.plain: Tobias's wedding was celebrated with gladness for seven days.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete (no verse 11:19)
readings.en: (nothing)

why: This is a real gap in Sinaiticus, not a numbering difference: its 11:18 matches Vaticanus 11:18, and nothing in it matches 11:19. But Sinaiticus 12:1 begins "When the wedding feast was over," which assumes a feast in Nineveh, so the Plain supplies the line from Vaticanus. The Vulgate, made from a different Aramaic copy, also has seven days of feasting.

a: Prayer joined with truth is good
t: Prayer with truth, or prayer with fasting?
p: Sinaiticus pairs prayer with truth. Vaticanus and the Vulgate pair it with fasting, giving the triad prayer, fasting and alms.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἀγαθὸν προσευχὴ μετὰ ἀληθείας
readings.en: prayer with truth is good
readings.plain: Prayer joined with truth is good

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: ἀγαθὸν προσευχὴ μετὰ νηστείας καὶ ἐλεημοσύνης καὶ δικαιοσύνης
readings.en: prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness
readings.plain: Prayer is good with fasting, alms and doing what is right

readings.w: Latin Vulgate and Douay-Rheims
readings.orig: Bona est oratio cum jejunio
readings.en: prayer is good with fasting
readings.plain: Prayer is good with fasting

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus, whose "truth" matches the book's language (prayer and service "in truth", 14:7, 14:9). The two Greek words ἀληθείας and νηστείας differ by a few letters. The Vaticanus and Vulgate reading matters for Christian practice: prayer, fasting and almsgiving are the three works of Matthew 6:1–18 and of the Catholic and Orthodox Lent, and Catholic teaching names them together (Catechism 1434).

a: but went off and wrapped the dead man for burial,
p: Vaticanus adds that Tobit's good deed was not hidden from the angel, who was with him.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ ᾤχου καὶ περιέστειλες τὸν νεκρόν
readings.en: and you went and wrapped the dead man
readings.plain: but went off and wrapped the dead man for burial,

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: ὅπως ἀπελθὼν περιστείλῃς τὸν νεκρόν, οὐκ ἔλαθές με ἀγαθοποιῶν, ἀλλὰ σὺν σοὶ ἤμην
readings.en: so as to go and wrap the dead man, your good deed was not hidden from me; I was with you
readings.plain: to go and wrap the dead man for burial, your good deed was not hidden from me: I was with you.

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. The Vaticanus line, followed by the KJV, makes Raphael a witness who was present at Tobit's good deeds, which readers have linked to the idea of a guardian angel (see the card at chapter 5).

a: it was then that I was sent to put you to the test.
p: Only Sinaiticus says Raphael was sent to test Tobit. The Vulgate has its own, famous version.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: τότε ἀπέσταλμαι ἐπὶ σὲ πειράσαι σε
readings.en: then I was sent to you to test you
readings.plain: it was then that I was sent to put you to the test.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: καὶ νῦν ἀπέστειλέν με ὁ θεὸς … (no testing)
readings.en: and now God has sent me … (no mention of testing)

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (12:13) and Douay-Rheims
readings.orig: quia acceptus eras Deo, necesse fuit ut tentatio probaret te
readings.en: because thou wast acceptable to God, it was necessary that temptation should prove thee
readings.plain: because you were pleasing to God, it was necessary that testing should prove you.

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. Vaticanus says only that Raphael "was with" Tobit in his good deeds and was sent to heal him. The Vulgate's line, which explains suffering as the proof of those God loves, entered Catholic spiritual writing through the Douay and older Latin Bibles.

a: to heal you and Sarah
p: Sinaiticus has "to heal, and Sarah" with no "you." Vaticanus names Tobit.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: ἰάσασθαί σε καὶ τὴν νύμφην σου Σάρραν
readings.en: to heal you and your daughter-in-law Sarah
readings.plain: to heal you and Sarah

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἰάσασθαι καὶ Σάρραν
readings.en: to heal, and Sarah too
readings.plain: to heal Sarah too

why: The Plain supplies "you" with Vaticanus. In Sinaiticus the "you" of "to test you" just before is probably meant to carry over, so the sense is the same: Raphael was sent to heal Tobit and Sarah.

a: one of the seven angels who stand in attendance and go in before the glory of the Lord
t: Do the seven angels bring up the prayers?
p: Vaticanus adds that the seven angels "bring up the prayers of the saints"; Sinaiticus does not.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: εἷς τῶν ἑπτὰ ἀγγέλων οἳ παρεστήκασιν καὶ εἰσπορεύονται ἐνώπιον τῆς δόξης Κυρίου
readings.en: one of the seven angels who stand by and go in before the glory of the Lord
readings.plain: one of the seven angels who stand in attendance and go in before the glory of the Lord

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: εἷς ἐκ τῶν ἑπτὰ ἁγίων ἀγγέλων οἳ προσαναφέρουσιν τὰς προσευχὰς τῶν ἁγίων καὶ εἰσπορεύονται ἐνώπιον τῆς δόξης τοῦ ἁγίου
readings.en: one of the seven holy angels who present the prayers of the saints and go in before the glory of the Holy One
readings.plain: one of the seven holy angels who present the prayers of the saints and go in before the glory of the Holy One

readings.w: Latin Vulgate and Douay-Rheims
readings.orig: unus ex septem qui adstamus ante Dominum
readings.en: one of the seven, who stand before the Lord
readings.plain: one of the seven who stand before the Lord

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus, which the Vulgate's shorter wording also supports. The Vaticanus phrase "present the prayers of the saints," followed by the KJV, is close to Revelation 8:3–4, where an angel offers incense with the prayers of God's people. It may be a fuller wording of 12:12 ("I carried the memorial of your prayer"). The idea is in both texts; only the phrase in this verse differs.

a: Now you see that I never ate anything; you were seeing a vision.
p: Vaticanus adds "or drink" and "all the days I appeared to you." The Vulgate speaks of invisible food.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: θεωρεῖτέ με ὅτι οὐκ ἔφαγον οὐθέν, ἀλλὰ ὅρασις ὑμῖν ἐθεωρεῖτο
readings.en: you see me, that I ate nothing, but a vision was seen by you
readings.plain: Now you see that I never ate anything; you were seeing a vision.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας ὠπτανόμην ὑμῖν, καὶ οὐκ ἔφαγον οὐδὲ ἔπιον, ἀλλὰ ὅρασιν ὑμεῖς ἐθεωρεῖτε
readings.en: all the days I appeared to you, and I did not eat or drink, but you saw a vision
readings.plain: All these days I appeared to you, but I did not eat or drink; you were seeing a vision.

readings.w: Latin Vulgate and Douay-Rheims
readings.orig: Videbar quidem vobiscum manducare et bibere: sed ego cibo invisibili, et potu qui ab hominibus videri non potest, utor
readings.en: I seemed indeed to eat and to drink with you but I use an invisible meat and drink, which cannot be seen by men
readings.plain: I seemed to eat and drink with you, but I use an invisible food and drink that people cannot see.

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. All three forms agree that the angel only appeared to eat.

a: Then Tobit said:
p: Vaticanus, followed by the KJV, says that Tobit "wrote a prayer of rejoicing."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Καὶ εἶπεν
readings.en: and he said
readings.plain: Then Tobit said:

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: Καὶ Τωβεὶτ ἔγραψεν προσευχὴν εἰς ἀγαλλίασιν καὶ εἶπεν
readings.en: and Tobit wrote a prayer for rejoicing and said
readings.plain: Then Tobit wrote a prayer of rejoicing and said:

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus, naming Tobit for clarity. The Vaticanus title links the hymn to Raphael's command to write everything down (12:20).

a: thank him with your whole mouth
p: Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus say "with your whole mouth"; Vaticanus "with your whole body."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete; Codex Alexandrinus (A)
readings.orig: ἐξομολογήσασθε αὐτῷ ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ στόματι ὑμῶν
readings.en: give thanks to him with your whole mouth
readings.plain: thank him with your whole mouth

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἐξομολογήσασθε αὐτῷ ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν
readings.en: give thanks to him with your whole body
readings.plain: thank him with your whole body

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus, which Alexandrinus supports (Swete's note on 13:6). The words στόματι and σώματι differ by one letter. In 11:15 Sinaiticus itself says Tobias blessed God "with his whole body," so either is possible; the KJV has "whole mouth."

a: Here in the land where I am a captive I thank him,
p: Sinaiticus lacks the end of 13:6 (the four lines from here on) and all of 13:7–9. The Plain follows Vaticanus there. This entry goes with those on 13:7, 13:8, 13:9 and 13:10.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: ἐγὼ ἐν τῇ γῇ τῆς αἰχμαλωσίας μου ἐξομολογοῦμαι αὐτῷ …
readings.en: I in the land of my captivity give him thanks …
readings.plain: Here in the land where I am a captive I thank him,

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete (text breaks off)
readings.en: (nothing)

why: Sinaiticus goes from the middle of 13:6 to the middle of 13:10. The missing lines both begin and end close to similar words, so it is usually explained as a copyist's eye skipping from one to the other. Swete prints the gap and gives the Vaticanus text, which the Plain follows.

a: I lift high my God,

p: As written, Sinaiticus says "he will settle all the farthest of the earth," which does not fit the line. The Plain reads one word as "inhabitants."

p: Sinaiticus curses those who speak harshly and those who destroy Jerusalem. Vaticanus has a short pair: a curse on those who hate the city, a blessing on those who love it.

a: the city that is his house, for all the ages.
p: Sinaiticus has "Jerusalem will be built, for the city, his house, for all ages," which does not quite hold together. Vaticanus has a different line.

why: The Greek of Sinaiticus has a bare "for the city" and then "his house" with no verb, so any translation must choose. The Plain takes the city and God's house as one, as in 14:5, where the house of God is built in the rebuilt Jerusalem. Others read "his house in the city." Vaticanus has no such line; it goes straight to the jewels.

p: Sinaiticus has the houses of Jerusalem cry Hallelujah; Vaticanus and the Vulgate have its streets.

p: Sinaiticus gives 112 years. Vaticanus gives Tobit's death later, at 158 (14:11). The Vulgate has 102.

a: the things Nahum spoke
p: Sinaiticus names Nahum. Vaticanus, Alexandrinus and the KJV name Jonah, here and in 14:8.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἃ ἐλάλησεν Ναούμ

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus. Nahum prophesied Nineveh's fall; Jonah's warning was withdrawn when the city repented (Jonah 3:4–10). "Jonah" is the easier reading for a copyist who thought of Jonah as the prophet of Nineveh, and Josephus shows that some Jews did connect Jonah with Nineveh's fall. Most recent commentators, among them Fitzmyer and Moore, read Nahum. Vaticanus repeats Jonah in 14:8 ("what the prophet Jonah said will surely happen"), where Sinaiticus names no prophet.

a: In those days every Israelite who is saved and keeps God faithfully in mind will be gathered in. They will come to Jerusalem and live securely for all time in Abraham's land, and it will be given into their hands. Those who love God in truth will be glad, while those who do sin and wrong will disappear from the whole earth.
t: The gathering of Israel, or the nations' praise?
p: Sinaiticus foretells the gathering of Israel to Jerusalem and the land. Vaticanus, followed by the KJV, speaks only of the nations' praise and of God lifting up his people.

readings.plain: In those days every Israelite who is saved and keeps God faithfully in mind will be gathered in. They will come to Jerusalem and live securely for all time in Abraham's land, and it will be given into their hands. Those who love God in truth will be glad, while those who do sin and wrong will disappear from the whole earth.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV

a: Now, children, here is my command to you: be God's servants in truth, and do what he finds pleasing. Teach your children too that they must do what is right and give alms, keep God in mind, and bless his name at every time, truthfully and with all their strength.
t: Tobit's command: to the children, or to Tobias?
p: Sinaiticus addresses the children and tells them to teach their own children. Vaticanus, followed by the KJV, tells Tobias to keep the law and be merciful and just.

readings.plain: Now, children, here is my command to you: be God's servants in truth, and do what he finds pleasing. Teach your children too that they must do what is right and give alms, keep God in mind, and bless his name at every time, truthfully and with all their strength.

a: how Nadab treated Ahiqar
p: The villain's name varies: Nadab in Sinaiticus, Adam in Vaticanus, Aman in the KJV.

readings.orig: ὅσα Ναδὰβ ἐποίησεν Ἀχεικάρῳ

readings.plain: how Nadab treated Ahiqar

readings.plain: how Adam treated Ahiqar

readings.w: King James Version (1611), from other Greek copies
readings.orig: Aman
readings.en: how Aman handled Achiacharus (Ahiqar)
readings.plain: how Aman treated Ahiqar

why: The Plain follows Sinaiticus, whose Nadab matches the nephew of 11:18 and is close to Nadin, the nephew's name in the Aramaic Story of Ahiqar. "Adam" in Vaticanus looks like a copying slip, and the KJV's "Aman" (Haman) may come from copyists who thought of Esther's villain.

a: Because Ahiqar gave alms
t: Who gave alms: "I," Ahiqar or Manasseh?
p: Sinaiticus literally says "because I gave alms." Vaticanus says "Manasseh gave alms."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete, taken as Ahiqar
readings.orig: ἐν τῷ ποιῆσαί με ἐλεημοσύνην ἐξῆλθεν ἐκ τῆς παγίδος τοῦ θανάτου
readings.en: in my doing alms he came out of the trap of death
readings.plain: Because Ahiqar gave alms

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), the longer Greek text, as printed by Swete, read word for word
readings.orig: ἐν τῷ ποιῆσαί με ἐλεημοσύνην
readings.en: because I gave alms
readings.plain: Because I gave alms

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), the shorter Greek text, as printed by Swete; KJV
readings.orig: Μανασσῆς ἐποίησεν ἐλεημοσύνην, καὶ ἐσώθη ἐκ παγίδος θανάτου
readings.en: Manasseh gave alms and was saved from the trap of death
readings.plain: Because Manasseh gave alms

why: The Sinaiticus "I" (με) makes no clear sense in Tobit's mouth; it may be Ahiqar's own words quoted, or a copyist's slip. The Plain takes it as Ahiqar's almsgiving, which fits the Story of Ahiqar, where he is saved by an officer whose life he had once spared, and Tobit's point in 14:11. This is an interpretation, so both literal readings are given. Vaticanus's "Manasseh" may be a garbled form of a name in the Ahiqar story; scholars are unsure.

t: Wrongdoing kills, or right deeds rescue?
p: Sinaiticus sets alms against wrongdoing, which kills. Vaticanus sets alms beside right deeds, which rescue.

readings.orig: Ναβουχοδονοσὸρ καὶ Ἀσύηρος
readings.en: Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus
readings.plain: Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus

why: The Plain prints what the first scribe of Sinaiticus wrote. Historically, Nineveh fell in 612 BC to Nabopolassar of Babylon and Cyaxares of Media. "Achiacharus" is spelled exactly as Vaticanus spells Ahiqar, and is probably a confusion with Cyaxares (Greek Kyaxarēs), so many modern translations print "Cyaxares," an editor's correction. Nebuchadnezzar was Nabopolassar's son, and "Ahasuerus" may be another garbled form of Cyaxares.
